1.pericope_label: The seventh seal opened: silence in heaven about the space of half an hour

schools.summary: Say first that the verse is misplaced by the chapter division: the section it belongs to is the one before, since the second verse begins a new series of visions and this one closes the old. Then face the question the seventh seal raises, whether the sealed roll is ever unrolled at all. The view that the visions merely accompany the openings and the roll is never read is singularly harsh, for the book was seen in the hand of him on the throne, the seer longed to know its contents, wept when no one could open it, and was comforted by hearing that the Lion of Judah had prevailed — and on that reading not a line is ever revealed, of which John gives no hint. Only a spirit in bondage to foolish literalisms asks how visions can be the writing in a roll. Describe the effect of the silence rather than assigning it a cause: no elder or angel speaking, no chorus of praise, no thunder from the throne, but a temporary cessation in the revelations; and note that the word for the half hour is late, rare and found here alone.

Take the silence as a metaphor for solemn expectation, on the ordinary observation that when something prodigious is looked for all is still and the breath is scarcely heard to be drawn. Then ground it in the temple service, which this chapter alludes to so strongly as to presume the temple still standing: on the Day of Atonement the high priest took fire from the great altar in a golden censer rather than a silver one, and while he offered the incense the people prayed outside in silence — which is the silence in heaven for half an hour, and which explains why the angel who follows appears to execute a priest's office. And say what the silence is for: it is only a preparation, and the grand point is the sounding of the trumpets. Mark how remarkable it is, since praise sounds in heaven day and night, and immediately before this the angels and the innumerable multitude had been crying with a loud voice, so that all is still at once and there is an universal pause.

Set the seal in its place in the chain: this opening introduces a new set of prophetic images, and there is a continued chain of providence in which one part is linked to another, where one ends another begins, so that things differing in nature and in time make up one well-connected design. On the silence itself offer two readings without forcing a choice — a silence of peace, since no complaints were going up to the ear of the Lord of sabaoth and all was quiet in the church, or a silence of expectation, great things being on the wheel of providence and the church standing still to see what God was doing, as when all flesh is bidden be silent before the Lord.

Give the silence a reason drawn from the shape of the book itself: it signifies the beginning of everlasting rest, but is described as partial and interrupted, because if the silence had continued here would be the end of the narrative. Then set the seals in order against the days of the week: at the sixth seal the greatest afflictions of the Church, at the seventh rest, since the Lord was crucified on the sixth day and rested on the Sabbath awaiting the resurrection. Report the reckoning of the forty-five days beyond Daniel's twelve hundred and ninety, as Jerome interpreted them, and confess that why there should be silence for those days is a matter of divine knowledge, unless the deferring of the kingdom of the saints is the trial of patience. And warn the reader that what follows is a recapitulation, the same things about to be said in another manner.

debates.question: What does the half-hour silence signify?

sides.position: Solemn expectation, on the analogy of the temple, where the people prayed outside in silence while the priest offered incense
Either a silence of peace, no complaints going up because all was quiet in the church, or a silence of expectation — the choice left open
A preparation only, remarkable because praise sounds in heaven day and night and the loud crying had just ceased; the grand point is the trumpets that follow
The beginning of everlasting rest, described as partial because a continued silence would have ended the narrative
A real interval after the death of Antichrist, answering to the forty-five days beyond Daniel's reckoning

outliers.note: Alone objects that the verse has been wrongly prefixed to this chapter, belonging with the section before it; and alone argues at length against the view that the sealed roll is never unrolled, on the ground that the narrative builds up an expectation which that reading leaves permanently unsatisfied, of which John himself gives no hint.

Alone ties the silence to a specific rite, the golden censer of the day of expiation and the people praying outside while the priest offered incense, and alone draws from the chapter's temple imagery the inference that the temple was still standing when it was written.

Alone reads the seals against the days of the week — the greatest afflictions at the sixth, rest at the seventh, since the Lord was crucified on the sixth day and rested on the Sabbath — and alone warns that what follows is a recapitulation rather than a continuation.

Alone explains the brevity of the silence by the requirements of the book itself, that it is described as partial and interrupted because a continued silence would have brought the narrative to an end.

themes: And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour.

2.pericope_label: Seven angels which stood before God, and seven trumpets given to them

schools.summary: The difficulty is the definite article, since the seven angels reads as though they had been introduced already. Two answers are possible and both are worth giving. Either it points to seven well-known figures — Enoch names seven archangels, and angels of the Presence is an idea with an Old Testament root, though we do not know precisely what John had in mind — or the article does not imply prior mention at all, since one may speak of the seven members of a cabinet without having introduced them, and standing before God may itself be definite enough, as Gabriel says he stands in the presence of God. Then set out the architecture of what follows, because it governs the reading of four chapters. The trumpet visions are arranged in marked correspondence with the seals: in each series two subordinate visions are interposed towards the end, giving an insight into the life within the life of Christ's Church where the main visions show the external aspects; and in each the first four are grouped against the last three, the first four trumpets falling on natural objects and the last three announced as woes.

Work through the candidates by elimination. Not the seven spirits of God, whose names and office differ; not the ministers of the word, though this book often calls them angels and they do blow the trumpet of the gospel; but angelic spirits, and either evil ones, since they execute wrath and bring judgements on the earth, or rather good angels, who are themselves sometimes ministers of divine wrath. Seven is the proper number for seven trumpets, and there may be an allusion to the seven princes whom eastern monarchs kept continually about them.

State the chronological rule that governs the whole book, since this verse forces it. The trumpets belong to the seventh seal as the vials belong to the seventh trumpet, and the parts must not be confounded; but it is not a certain rule that each part is fully accomplished before the next begins. Only the beginning of each goes before the beginning of the following, so that the epistles begin before the seals, the seals before the trumpets, the trumpets before the vials — and what begins later may end sooner, or begin earlier and end later, the seventh trumpet beginning before the vials and extending beyond them all. Note that the place of the first four is specified in turn, east and west and south and north. On the instrument, observe that when men wish to make a public matter known they give a token seen or heard far and wide, and none is more ancient than the trumpet, which Israel used in worship and in war alike. And say plainly that these were angels properly so called, not men, as some have thought.

debates.question: Does the article in 'the seven angels' imply that they have been mentioned before?

sides.position: Yes: it seems to point to seven well-known angels, such as the seven archangels named in Enoch
No: the article need not imply prior mention, as with the seven members of a cabinet or the governors of the states; standing before God may itself be definite enough

outliers.note: Alone lays down a rule for reading the whole book's chronology, that only the beginning of each series precedes the beginning of the next, so that what begins later may end sooner and the seventh trumpet begins before the vials and extends beyond them all.

Alone maps the correspondence between the trumpet visions and the seal visions — two subordinate visions interposed near the end of each, and the first four grouped against the last three in both — and distinguishes their function, the main visions giving the external aspects of Church history and the interposed ones the inner and more spiritual.

Alone entertains the possibility that these are evil angels, on the ground that they execute wrath and bring judgements on the earth, before preferring good angels who are sometimes ministers of wrath; and alone hears behind the number the seven princes that eastern monarchs kept about them.

themes: And I saw the seven angels which stood before God; and to them were given seven trumpets.

3.pericope_label: The angel with the golden censer, and the prayers of all saints

schools.summary: Be honest about the limits of the evidence on the altar: the manuscripts differ between genitive and accusative, the word here seems to mean the altar of incense, and it is not clear that apocalyptic writing preserves the distinction between the two altars at all. On the identity of the angel, resist the question rather than answering it. The designation another angel tells against identifying him with Christ, and there is really no need to ask who the several angels are, the book being symbolical and the angels standing not for particular persons but for the agencies — personal, natural or supernatural — employed by him who sits on the throne. Render the clause about the incense as giving it to the prayers rather than offering it with them, and take the mingled column of smoke as the token that the prayers, no longer premature, are about to be answered. Then say what that means: these weak and imperfect prayers are invincible weapons, mightier than carnal ones, so that as Jericho fell without Israel striking a blow, the Israel of God is omnipotent through faithful prayer — the judgements that follow being not asked for by the Church but the result of its asking.

Clear the ground of the wilder identifications before offering your own: not a created angel such as Gabriel, and not any mere man — neither the pope whom Lyra proposed, nor Constantine with the counsel of Nice, nor the emperor Theodosius praying before his battle. Then keep the ritual detail exact, that the incense was laid on burning coals and the smoke rose like a cloud until the house was filled, and that the golden censer was the vessel for carrying those coals.

Two things must be decided here and they pull against each other. Take the angel as about to perform a priest's office, on the evidence of the day of expiation rite; but note also that the text does not say he offered the incense, only that he should give it, and that the incense ascends with the prayers of the saints and not for them, since angels are fellow servants with the saints and not mediators for them. On the smoke, observe that it is not said the angel presents the prayers at all: he presents the incense, and the prayers ascend with it, the ascent being the token that both were accepted. Take the incense itself for the longing desires of the angels that the counsel of God might be fulfilled, and settle the angel's identity by a rule drawn from the book, that in this part of the Revelation Christ is never called an angel but the Lamb.

debates.question: Is the angel discharging a priest's office?

sides.position: Yes: he is about to perform the office of priest, as the Day of Atonement rite of the golden censer shows
No: the text says he should give the incense, not offer it, and he discharges the office of an angel; angels are fellow servants with the saints, not mediators for them

debates.question: Which altar does he stand at?

sides.position: The golden altar of incense, though apocalyptic may not preserve the distinction between the two altars
The altar of burnt offerings

outliers.note: Alone refuses the question of the angel's identity on principle rather than answering it, holding that the book is symbolical and the angels stand for agencies rather than persons; and alone draws from the ascending incense the claim that the prayers of God's people are invincible weapons, so that as Jericho fell without a blow the Israel of God is omnipotent through prayer.

Alone settles the identity by a rule internal to the book, that in this part of the Revelation Christ is never termed an angel but the Lamb; and alone insists that the incense goes up with the prayers of the saints but not for them, angels being fellow servants and not mediators.

Alone marks the casting down of the censer as a reversal rather than a continuation, coals taken from the altar with no incense laid on them and flung to the earth as though prayer were now in vain, and finds the image in Ezekiel's man clothed in linen scattering coals over the city.

themes: And another angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer; and there was given unto him much incense, that he should offer it with the prayers of all saints upon the golden altar which was before the throne.
And the smoke of the incense, which came with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God out of the angel’s hand.
And the angel took the censer, and filled it with fire of the altar, and cast it into the earth: and there were voices, and thunderings, and lightnings, and an earthquake.

6.pericope_label: The first trumpet: hail and fire mingled with blood

schools.summary: Press the Egyptian parallel and then press the difference, because the difference decides the method. The plague of hail and fire that ran along the ground is plainly behind this, and the resemblance is meant to carry us back to the mighty works of God in old times; but this plague adds blood, and that variation takes the vision out of the possibility of literal interpretation, putting it with the figurative language of Joel about blood and fire and pillars of smoke, whose fulfilment Peter dated from Pentecost. Warn those who want limited historical fulfilments that the visions seem meant to show the general kind of event that marks the decay of the kingdom of wrong and the growth of the kingdom of Christ — landing stages in an advancing progress rather than dated occurrences. On the Greek, note that the verb for burning up is repeated three times for dramatic effect, and that the storm, in Swete's phrase, flung itself upon the earth.

Two things are needed here, a text and a caution. On the text, report that before the clause about the trees the Codex Alexandrinus and some thirty-five others, with the Syriac and Vulgate and much else, add that the third part of the land was burnt up — a reading that is undoubtedly genuine and which Griesbach admitted. On the caution: some fruitful imaginations might find gunpowder and cannon balls and canister shot and bombs in the hail and fire, and many eminent men suppose the barbarian irruption on the Roman empire is meant, but it is easy to find coincidences when fancy runs riot, and later writers might as well find here the Austrians and Prussians and Russians falling on the French empire. Read the vegetation as figure — the trees for the chiefs of a nation, the grass for the common people, so that high and low alike were overwhelmed — and if a historical application must be made, weigh the Jewish calamities under Trajan and Adrian, the rising of the year 114 and the war under Barcochab that left Judea desolate by 135.

debates.question: What historical event, if any, does the first trumpet denote?

sides.position: The invasion of Alaric and the Goths, the first of the great blows that brought down the Roman empire
The Jewish calamities under Trajan and Adrian, beginning with the insurrection of 114 and ending with the desolation of Judea in 135
None that can be identified: it is easy to find coincidences when fancy runs riot
No dated event at all; the visions show the general kind of occurrence that marks the decay of the kingdom of wrong

outliers.note: Alone ridicules the whole enterprise of historical identification, observing that fruitful imaginations might find gunpowder and cannon balls in the hail and fire, and that later writers might as easily find the Austrians and Prussians and Russians falling on the French empire; and alone reports the substantial addition to the text which Griesbach admitted.

Alone argues from the difference between this plague and the Egyptian one — the addition of blood — that the vision cannot be taken literally, and alone states the alternative method, that the visions are landing stages in an advancing progress rather than dated occurrences.

Alone works out a sustained historical identification, taking the first trumpet for the invasion of Alaric and referring the reader to Gibbon for the extent of the devastation, while allowing that the third part need not be exact.

themes: And the seven angels which had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound.
The first angel sounded, and there followed hail and fire mingled with blood, and they were cast upon the earth: and the third part of trees was burnt up, and all green grass was burnt up.

8.pericope_label: The second trumpet: a great mountain burning cast into the sea

schools.summary: Resist the political allegory long enough to read the words as they stand: it is not a great mountain but a blazing mass as large as one, and the picture behind it may be a volcanic eruption — Vesuvius in the year seventy-nine, or the eruption Strabo records which threw up a new island. The sea turning to blood recalls the first Egyptian plague, the Nile struck and the fish dying. If the allegorical reading is given, give it as what it is: a mountain is a natural symbol of strength, being defensible in itself and anciently a seat of power, and Jeremiah's destroying mountain and Daniel's stone that became a great mountain are the warrant for it. Keep the maritime sense of the judgement throughout, and insist that nothing here is literal — the effect described is as if a third of all that was in the sea perished, and the ships are naval armaments or vessels of commerce.
Read the creatures of the sea as men, the inhabitants of the empire, noting that the Targum understands fish in one place as mighty princes and governors.

Give the prophetic vocabulary first: a mountain in prophetic language signifies a kingdom, great disorders are figured by mountains cast into the sea, and seas and collections of waters mean peoples, as this book itself explains. Then decline the identification, since great commotions in kingdoms and among their inhabitants may be intended, but to whom, where and when these happened, or are to happen, we do not know. On the fraction, do not make it arithmetical: the third part is a rabbinism for a considerable number, as in the saying that when Rabbi Akiba prayed and wept and sat in the dust the world was struck with a curse and the third part of the olives and of the wheat and of the barley was smitten; and the words need not imply that exactly a third of the Romans was slain, only that an inconceivable deal of blood was shed.

sides.position: A strong nation, since a mountain is a natural symbol of a kingdom — specifically Genseric and the Vandals, whose power was maritime
A great force and multitude of people: the barbarian irruptions, the Goths breaking in about 250 and one nation following another until the empire was lost
Some great commotion among kingdoms, but to whom, where and when it happened or is to happen we do not know
Not a mountain at all but a blazing mass as large as one, perhaps with a volcanic eruption behind the picture

outliers.note: Alone declines the political allegory and reads the image naturally, as a blazing mass the size of a mountain, comparing the eruption of Vesuvius in A.D. 79 and the eruption recorded by Strabo which threw up a new island.
Alone treats the third part as a rabbinism for a considerable number rather than a fraction, quoting the saying about Rabbi Akiba and the third part of the olives and the wheat and the barley.

Alone defends his historical method against the charge of forcing the text, remarking that he had worked through the interpretation of the symbol's language before he looked into Gibbon with any reference to the application; and alone reaches for Paradise Lost, where the angels pluck the seated hills with all their load of rocks and waters and woods.

themes: And the second angel sounded, and as it were a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea: and the third part of the sea became blood;
And the third part of the creatures which were in the sea, and had life, died; and the third part of the ships were destroyed.

10.pericope_label: The third trumpet: the star Wormwood falls upon the rivers

schools.summary: Make one correction that carries weight: the star is kindled, not shining of itself, so the light is borrowed. Take the falling star as a natural emblem of a prince or ruler, one distinguished by rank or talent, and be exact about the kind of light — not a lurid or ghastly meteor but a bright and blazing one, emblem of fiery energy and rapid execution and splendour of appearance. Read the blast as proclaiming that the mighty who have been admired as luminaries, and perhaps worshipped, will fall; and note what the fall costs, since the fountains and rivers that are smitten are the sources of health and joy and the streams of prosperity. On the name, be precise: the noun is absinthe, usually feminine but masculine here because the star is, occurring nowhere else in the New Testament and not in the Greek Old Testament save in a later translator, though several varieties of the plant grow in Palestine. Supply the scriptural background, the people fed with wormwood and given water of gall, the root bearing gall and wormwood, and Moses grinding the golden calf to powder and making Israel drink it. Then decline to reduce the vision to a single false teacher: the main point is the general stages marking the advance of Christianity, and all such false lights shall fall before the true Light and Morning Star, who will heal the embittered waters of life.

The identifications on offer are many and mutually exclusive — Attila and his Huns, Genseric with his Vandals, the Eleazer who stirred the Zealots, Arius infecting the doctrine with his heresy — and the honest course is to say that it certainly cannot mean all of them and probably none of them, and let the reader judge. If the Arian reading is pressed, press it consistently: this star was not an angel, since angels are not the agents in the neighbouring trumpets, but a teacher of the church, one of the stars in Christ's right hand, who fell from on high into the most pernicious doctrines and made a gazing on all sides in his fall; the rivers are Africa, and Egypt in particular, which the Nile overflows yearly; and the bitterness of the title answers exactly to the bitterness of the man and his followers. Note carefully that many died, though not a third part of them.

debates.question: Who or what is the falling star?

sides.position: Attila, whose empire flared and was extinguished within a few years, as Gibbon relates
Arius: not an angel but a teacher of the church, one of the stars in Christ's right hand, whose doctrine spread through Africa and Egypt
None of the candidates proposed — Attila, Genseric, Eleazar, Arius: it certainly cannot mean all these, and probably none of them
No particular person, but the fall of potentates generally, which marks the advance of Christianity and brings misery in its train

outliers.note: Alone observes that the star is kindled rather than self-luminous, the light being borrowed; and alone grants that the false-teacher reading has support in the passages he cites while declining to make it the main point, ending instead on the true Light and Morning Star who will heal the embittered waters.

Alone rules out an angelic agent on structural grounds, that angels are not the agents in the neighbouring trumpets, and so identifies the star with a teacher of the church; and alone traces the consequences of Arianism through the invitation of the Vandals into Africa in 428 to the fall of their kingdom in 533.
Alone attends to the gender of the noun, usually feminine but masculine here because the star is, and notes that it is absent from the Greek Old Testament except in a later translator.

themes: And the third angel sounded, and there fell a great star from heaven, burning as it were a lamp, and it fell upon the third part of the rivers, and upon the fountains of waters;
And the name of the star is called Wormwood: and the third part of the waters became wormwood; and many men died of the waters, because they were made bitter.

12.pericope_label: The fourth trumpet, and the angel crying woe to the inhabiters of the earth

schools.summary: Mark the difference from the Egyptian plague as carefully as the likeness: there the darkness could be felt while Israel had light in their dwellings, whereas here it is only partial, a third of the sun's light withdrawn by day and of the moon and stars by night, which are far more needful in eastern lands than in ours. Hear in it the day of the Lord in which the light is neither clear nor dark, and the distress of nations with men's hearts failing them; and say that such times must come, since the Church goes forward through seasons when the lights of human wisdom and of spiritual guidance seem alike obscured. Then set the trumpets against Genesis, where they look like the undoing of creation — the vegetation smitten, the earth and sea intermingled, the lights of heaven darkened, the living things in seas and streams destroyed — and draw the conclusion, that chaos preceded creation and through chaos the Church must pass to the new heaven and new earth, the pulling down going before the building up. On the last verse, follow the better manuscripts and read a single eagle rather than an angel, flying in mid-heaven and therefore visible to the very horizon.

Report the candidates without adopting either: some refer the fourth trumpet to the Eutychian heresy, which confounded the two natures of Christ and so brought darkness on the doctrine of his person, and others to the darkness that preceded and introduced the papacy. On the last verse, list the witnesses for the variant — the Alexandrian copy, the Complutensian edition, the Vulgate, Syriac and Ethiopic all read eagle — while observing that flying suits either word and the sense is the same read which way you please.

Give the calendar, since the fourth trumpet is the extinction of the western empire: the Goths and Huns falling on Italy in 403 and 405, Rome stormed in 410, Attila serving the upper part of Italy the same way in 452, Genseric plundering Rome for a fortnight in 455, Recimer plundering it again in 472, and Odoacer deposing the emperor in 476. Support the figure with the observation that the Hebrews call an eclipse a stroke, and that since such darkness comes on by degrees rather than all at once, so did the darkness that fell on the Roman world, the stroke beginning long before Odoacer. Keep the figures consistent with the earlier trumpets: as earth and sea and rivers meant the men who inhabit them, so sun and moon and stars mean the men who live under them. On the last verse, prefer eagle to angel with almost every manuscript of note, and take the point of the bird — the eagle was the symbol of the Romans and stood always on their ensigns, so that the three woes were probably to be executed by that people.

debates.question: Does the last verse speak of an angel or an eagle?

sides.position: An eagle, on almost every manuscript and version of note; Griesbach admitted it, and the bird is the point, being the Roman ensign
The witnesses for eagle are real, but flying suits either and the sense is the same read which way you like
Angel, without remark on the variant; the interest lies in the grouping of the three remaining trumpets against the first four

outliers.note: Alone reads the four trumpets together against the story of Genesis and finds them an undoing of creation — vegetation smitten, earth and sea intermingled, the lights darkened, the living things destroyed — concluding that chaos preceded creation and through chaos the Church must pass to the new heaven and new earth.

Alone supports the figure with a point of Hebrew usage, that an eclipse is called a stroke, and argues from the gradualness of an eclipse that the darkness which fell on the western empire likewise came on by degrees, the stroke beginning long before Odoacer.

Alone makes the disputed reading do exegetical work, observing that the eagle was the symbol of the Romans and stood always on their ensigns, so that the three woes were probably to be executed by that people and upon the Jews.

themes: And the fourth angel sounded, and the third part of the sun was smitten, and the third part of the moon, and the third part of the stars; so as the third part of them was darkened, and the day shone not for a third part of it, and the night likewise.

And I beheld, and heard an angel flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice, Woe, woe, woe, to the inhabiters of the earth by reason of the other voices of the trumpet of the three angels, which are yet to sound!
